Planks
plăngks
n. pl. (thick boards of timber; in the temple, the fir flooring and the thick boards of the porch)
Old French planche, a board. Distinguished in the Authorized Version from boards, which are lighter, and from beams, which carry weight.

Biblical Definition

Solomon “built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir” (1Ki 6:15). Cedar on the walls, fir underfoot — and not one stone of the costly masonry left showing inside. The next verses say the cedar was carved with knops and open flowers, and that the whole house was overlaid with gold; the account is careful to add that there was no stone seen. In Ezekiel's visionary temple the planks return: “there were thick planks upon the face of the porch without” (Eze 41:25), and again with the narrow windows and the palm trees on the sides of the porch (Eze 41:26). Two chapters of a book written to exiles are given to measurements of a house they could not see, and the reason is stated at the end: shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern. God gives a precise design to a homeless people as a summons to holiness. Planks are humble things, and Scripture records them because the house of God is built out of humble things exactly specified.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a plank as a broad piece of sawed timber, differing from a board only in being thicker; and figuratively, that on which one stands or relies.

expand to see more

PLANK, n. A broad piece of sawed timber, differing from a board only in being thicker.

2. In seamen's language, planks are the thick boards with which a ship's side and deck are covered.

PLANK, v.t. To cover or lay with planks.

Key Scripture

1Ki 6:15 — "And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir."

Eze 41:25 — "And there were made on them, on the doors of the temple, cherubims and palm trees, like as were made upon the walls; and there were thick planks upon the face of the porch without."

1Ch 28:19 — "All this, said David, the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern."

Modern Corruption

The building chapters are skipped as tedious inventory, and with them goes the doctrine they exist to teach: that God specifies how He is to be approached and does not leave it to the builder's taste.

expand to see more

Whole chapters of Exodus, 1 Kings, and Ezekiel consist of measurements, materials, and joinery, and they are among the least-read pages in the Bible. The reason they are there is doctrinal, not decorative. David says of the temple plan, All this the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern (1Ch 28:19); Moses was warned of God when he was about to make the tabernacle, See that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount (Heb 8:5). The house in which God is approached is designed by God, down to the planks of fir on the floor. That principle survives the ceremonial law and appears in the New Testament as the regulative principle of worship, which the 1689 Confession states plainly: the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by Himself, and so limited by His own revealed will, that He may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scriptures. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and died for it; Uzzah steadied the ark with the best of intentions. Modern worship planning is very largely a discussion of taste, effect, and audience. The building chapters, tedious as they look, are the standing reminder that God has always told His people exactly how He would be approached.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsela' (H6763), a side, a board or plank; 'ets (H6086), wood, timber; berowsh (H1265), fir or cypress, the wood of the temple floor.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsela' (H6763) — a rib, a side, a plank or board; used of the boards of the temple and of the rib taken from Adam; 1 Kings 6:15, Genesis 2:22.

Hebrew berowsh (H1265) — fir or cypress; the flooring of Solomon's house and the timber Hiram sent from Lebanon; 1 Kings 6:15, 1 Kings 5:8.

Hebrew tabniyth (H8403) — a pattern, a model; the plan shewed to Moses in the mount and given to David in writing; Exodus 25:9, 1 Chronicles 28:19.

Usage

"“Covered the floor of the house with planks of fir” — and there was no stone seen."

"“Thick planks upon the face of the porch without” — a design given to exiles who could not build it."

"“All the works of this pattern” — the house of God is not left to the builder's taste."
